mode.description: "standard": the normal web search: quick and cheap; right for straightforward lookups (reference facts, official pages, documentation, well-known people, places and topics) and simple follow-up lookups. "extended": a thorough, fresh search at several times the cost and latency.

tools.name: Write
tools.description:
Writes a file to the local filesystem, overwriting if one exists.

When to use: creating a new file, or fully replacing one you've already Read. Overwriting an existing file you haven't Read will fail. For partial changes, use Edit instead.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to write (must be absolute, not relative)

content.description: The content to write to the file

tools.name: mcp__1a59c906-04da-521d-bda7-7f71b9f9e01c__batch
tools.description: Create a doc, or apply several operations to one doc atomically.

tools.name: mcp__1a59c906-04da-521d-bda7-7f71b9f9e01c__guide
tools.description: Docs guides: topic.instructions repeats the server instructions. Read it only if your client dropped them. Also topic.<name>, refusal.<code>. After a doc's birth → ["topic.index"].

items.description: topic.<name> (instructions, index, editing, tabs, comments, charts, chart-definition, diagram, uploads, sharing, skill) or refusal.<code>; several per call is fine.

tools.name: mcp__1a59c906-04da-521d-bda7-7f71b9f9e01c__update
tools.description: Edit a tab's contents, rename a doc or tab, or change a stored value. Rename a doc only when asked to, not to change a link's text. It may be one the given doc links to: read its tabs' text to see links.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__dismiss_task
tools.description:
Withdraw a proposal you made with start_session (initiation "own_initiative" or "offer") that the user has not started.

Call this when it went stale: the work was done here after all (by you or the user), it turned out unnecessary, or you proposed a better-scoped replacement (propose the new one first, then dismiss the old task_id). A card the user answered has already left, "Do it here" included, so it needs no call.

Read the result before you start the task anew or do it here: after "Not withdrawn", do neither.

task_id.description: The task_id the start_session proposal returned.

reason.description: Optional one-line reason the suggestion is no longer needed, e.g. "fixed in this session" or "superseded by task_ab12cd34".

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__hand_off_to_session
tools.description: Move the task you are in the middle of into its own session (a fork of this conversation plus your remaining plan) so you can answer the user now. Use it when a new user message about something else arrives mid-task — not for small corrections or when the user said to keep the work here. In a worktree the fork gets a fresh worktree, normally cut from your branch tip: commit first (uncommitted edits stay here). Bold title line and one sentence right before the call; after it, stop that task here and answer the new message — no recap.

title.description: Under 60 chars; names the task being moved.

remaining_plan.description: What is left to do: steps, files, what done looks like.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__mark_chapter
tools.description:
Mark the start of a new chapter in this session.

Call this when the work shifts to a meaningfully different phase — e.g. after finishing exploration and starting implementation, after a fix lands and you move to verification, or when the user pivots to an unrelated request. The user sees a divider in the transcript and a floating table of contents for jumping between chapters.

Use sparingly: a chapter should cover a coherent stretch of work, not every tool call. A typical session has 3–8 chapters. Do not mark a chapter for the very first message — the session start is implicit.

The title is a short noun phrase ("Codebase exploration", "Auth bug fix", "Test verification"), not a sentence.

title.description: Short noun-phrase title for the chapter (under 40 chars). Shown in the table of contents.

summary.description: Optional one-line summary of what this chapter covers. Shown on hover in the table of contents.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__read_widget_context
tools.description: Read context from an embedded interactive widget. Widgets are rendered alongside chat from prior tool calls and can be interacted with by the user. Call this when you need to know the current state of a widget.

tool_name.description: The name of the widget tool to get context for

tools.name: mcp__ccd_turn__update_plan
tools.description:
Keep the task list the app shows under your latest message while you work. Every request that edits files or runs more than one command gets one (implement-and-test, investigate-then-fix, anything the user listed); only a single-command answer or pure conversation does not.

Never spend a message on this tool alone: send it IN THE SAME MESSAGE as another tool call (in parallel), so it costs no extra round trip.
- First call: with the VERY FIRST tool call of the turn, even one that only reads or lists files: {"items": [...]}, the whole plan in order, short imperative phrases (at most ~7 words, no numbering), the step you are starting "in_progress", the rest "pending". If you must look around first, make "Look at how X is set up" step one and refine the list once you know.
- Next step: {"advance": true} alongside the call that begins it (completes the in_progress step, starts the next pending one); after the last step, advance alongside wrap_up.
- Out of order: {"done": [2], "start": 4} (1-based).
- Plan changed, including right after the user interrupts or sends a new instruction mid-task: {"items": [...]} again, the new whole list, so the pinned list never shows an abandoned plan.
- Every {"items"} call says in "scope" what this request is to the session: "first_task" (nothing finished here yet); after that, "new_task" (unrelated work: it builds on nothing done, found or decided here) or "continuation" (everything else: anything a few tool calls settle, the next iteration, acting on what you just investigated or suggested, even if that work gets its own commit or PR; when unsure, this one). A "new_task" turn opens with a start_session offer and reaches this call only if the user chose Do it here.
Keep exactly one step in_progress while working and none when everything is done. Do not also write the plan as a numbered list in your message: the pinned list is the plan.

scope.description: Required with items: "first_task", "continuation" or "new_task" (see the tool description). Omit on advance / done / start updates.

session.description: When you delegated this step to a session you started: that session's short name (from start_session's result). The app shows its live state on the step.

items.description: The whole plan, in order (1–12 steps); replaces the previous list.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_turn__wrap_up
tools.description:
Fill the "next step" box the app shows at the end of your turn: a two-or-three-sentence recap and, when this turn leaves the user a decision to make or a step to take, one question and buttons that answer it; a turn with nothing pending ends with the recap alone, and the app then draws no box. Call it once in EVERY turn in which you kept a task list, changed files, ran commands, or completed multi-step work: when this turn's work is done, before any closing message (it also checks off the task list; no closing update_plan is needed). Skip it for short answers, pure conversation, or a brief read-and-explain turn — a reply that names a follow-up is not brief: ask or propose it, and call this.

Your closing message is ordinary text right after this call, the last thing you say this turn: your answer to the user in full, which the recap never replaces. Never write it before this call, where it can reach the user cut to a short summary. The result says whether the box shows your question: ask in the message only a question it does not show.

Fields (write recap last) — ask and recap are said to the user, in the second person; a reply button's label is the user's words back to you:
- ask (with actions, only when the next move is the user's call — a choice of approach, a go-ahead to fix, commit, push, post or send, an approval): just that ONE decision in one short sentence, never two joined by "and" ("Which fix first?"), with no reason or recommendation and without listing the options the buttons give: your pick, actions[0], is drawn as the primary button. At most 100 characters.
- recap: what is now true or changed, then where it stands, including what is not done or not verified (for example: nothing committed, or not checked in the app). Two or three short sentences, about 40 words / 300 characters, in the project's own words. No recommendation here.
Every field is a top-level parameter holding plain prose (actions: a JSON array); none contains markup or another field.

ask.description: The one question (≤100 chars) when the next move is the user's call — a choice, a go-ahead (to act here on what this turn found, say), an approval: the decision alone, with no reason or recommendation and without listing the options the buttons give (actions[0] is your pick). Like the recap, never point at anything else in the conversation. Omit it, and actions, when nothing waits on the user.

blocked.description: true when your work stops here until the user answers (the app marks the session as waiting on them); omit when the answer can wait.

action.description: An app action update_plan's result listed as available, or one your own work this turn made available; others are refused, and one that later stops being available is dropped (as actions[0], with your ask and other answers), so do not guess. Offer commit, create_pr or verify only once the work the user asked for is done, not every turn. Omit for a reply.

label.description: For a reply: the button text, 1–3 words (4 only when three cannot say it) / 24 characters — "Yes, fix 1", "Not now": a button, not a sentence. A click sends it to you as the user's answer. Never a go-ahead to commit: that is the commit app action. No leading / or !. Ignored for an app action.

actions.description: 1–2 buttons, recommendation first. They are answers to your ask: the first accepts your recommendation, and another is there only when it is a realistic alternative the user might pick instead — not a menu of everything you mentioned. When blocked is true, they are the most likely answers to your question. While Auto-fix is on for the session's PR, none offers to watch it, fix CI, resolve conflicts or address comments. Never repeat an offer the user passed over, as an app action, a reply or a question in your closing message, unless what it acts on has changed since or they bring it up.

recap.description: Two or three short sentences to the user (≤300 chars): what is now true or changed, then where it stands, including what is not done or not verified. Its first sentence is the sidebar status. It must stand on its own, since it is also read away from the transcript and the box draws under anything you write after this call: never point at anything else in the conversation ("listed below", "see above", "in my message").

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__browser_batch
tools.description: Execute a sequence of Browser pane tool calls in ONE round trip. Each item is {name, input} where input is exactly what you'd pass to that tool standalone. Actions execute SEQUENTIALLY (not in parallel) and stop on the first error. Use this tool extensively to quickly execute work whenever you can predict two or more steps ahead — e.g. navigate, click a field, type, press Return, screenshot. Each tool's own permission check runs per item — a step on a site the user hasn't allowed either asks the user inline (and continues if they allow) or is refused, which stops the batch; if a step is refused for a missing permission, call that tool on its own (that call can ask the user), then batch the rest. Screenshots and other images are returned interleaved with outputs; coordinates you write in THIS batch refer to the screenshot taken BEFORE this call. browser_batch cannot be nested, and preview_start is not batchable — but if the Browser pane isn't open yet, a batch whose FIRST action is navigate with a url opens it (other actions still need an open page).

name.description: Tool name (e.g. computer, navigate, find, form_input, read_page). browser_batch cannot be nested. A tabs_create's new tabId is only returned when the batch ends — load that tab in a later call.

input.description: That tool's input — same shape you'd pass when calling it directly. For computer items whose action is left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key or type, and for form_input items, include action_summary in the item's input, as you would when calling that tool directly.

actions.description: List of tool calls to execute sequentially. Example: [{"name":"computer","input":{"action":"left_click","ref":"ref_12"}},{"name":"computer","input":{"action":"type","text":"hello"}},{"name":"computer","input":{"action":"screenshot"}}]

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
tools.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

action.description:
The action to perform:
* `left_click`: Click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `right_click`: Click the right mouse button at the specified coordinates to open context menus.
* `double_click`: Double-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `triple_click`: Triple-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `type`: Type a string of text.
* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

coordinate.description: (x, y): The x (pixels from the left edge) and y (pixels from the top edge) coordinates. Required for `left_click`, `right_click`, `double_click`, `triple_click`, and `scroll`. For `left_click_drag`, this is the end position.

text.description: The text to type (for `type` action) or the key(s) to press (for `key` action). For `key` action: Provide space-separated keys (e.g., "Backspace Backspace Delete"). Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

duration.description: The number of seconds to wait. Required for `wait`. Maximum 10 seconds.

scroll_direction.description: The direction to scroll. Required for `scroll`.

scroll_amount.description: The number of scroll wheel ticks. Optional for `scroll`, defaults to 3.

region.description: (x0, y0, x1, y1): The rectangular region to capture for `zoom`. Coordinates define a rectangle from top-left (x0, y0) to bottom-right (x1, y1) in pixels from the viewport origin. Required for `zoom` action. Useful for inspecting small UI elements like icons, buttons, or text.

scale.description: For `screenshot` and `zoom` only. Scale factor in [0.1, 1] for the returned image; 1 (default) uses the full image token budget, 0.5 returns an image at half the width and height (~quarter of the tokens). Coordinates are ALWAYS in the full-resolution coordinate frame (reported with every scaled screenshot), never in the scaled image's own pixels.

repeat.description: Number of times to repeat the key sequence. Only applicable for `key` action. Must be a positive integer between 1 and 100. Default is 1. Useful for navigation tasks like pressing arrow keys multiple times.

ref.description: Element reference ID from read_page or find tools (e.g., "ref_1", "ref_2"). Required for `scroll_to` action. Can be used as alternative to `coordinate` for click actions.

modifiers.description: Modifier keys for click actions. Supports: "ctrl", "shift", "alt", "cmd" (or "meta"), "win" (or "windows"). Can be combined with "+" (e.g., "ctrl+shift", "cmd+alt"). Optional.

action_summary.description: A few words saying what this action does on the page and to what, for example 'Sends the drafted reply to pat@example.com' or 'Opens the Filters menu'. Set it on every left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key and type action. State the effect only, and accurately: no reasons, nothing about what you were asked or allowed to do, no passwords or other secrets.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__find
tools.description: Search the current page in the Browser pane for elements whose accessibility-tree line (role / name / text) contains `query`, case-insensitively. Returns up to 20 `ref_N` matches usable with `computer`/`form_input`.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

query.description: Text to look for in an element's role, name or text (case-insensitive substring, e.g. "Sign in", "search", "Add to cart").

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__form_input
tools.description: Set the value of a form element identified by `ref` (from read_page/find). Handles input/textarea/select/checkbox/contenteditable.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

ref.description: Element reference ID from the read_page tool (e.g., "ref_1", "ref_2")

value.description: The value to set. For checkboxes use boolean, for selects use option value or text, for other inputs use appropriate string/number

action_summary.description: A few words saying what this form fill does on the page and to what, for example 'Sets the delivery date to 29 September'. State the effect only, and accurately: no reasons, nothing about what you were asked or allowed to do, no passwords or other secrets.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__get_page_text
tools.description: Extract the visible text of the Browser pane's page (article/main content first, falls back to body innerText).

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__javascript_tool
tools.description: Execute JavaScript in the Browser pane's page for DEBUGGING and INSPECTION only. Do NOT use this to implement UI changes — edit source code instead.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

action.description: Action to perform (only `javascript_exec` is supported).

text.description: The JavaScript code to execute. Evaluated in the page context with REPL semantics: top-level `await` works, and the result of the last expression is returned automatically — write the expression you want (e.g. `window.myData.value`, or `await fetch(url).then(r=>r.json())`) rather than `return ...`. Return values are serialized as JSON.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__navigate
tools.description: Navigate the Browser pane to a URL, or go "back"/"forward" in history. If the Browser pane isn't open yet, this opens it at the URL (no dev server needed).

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

url.description: The URL to navigate to. Can be provided with or without protocol (defaults to https://). Use "forward" to go forward in history or "back" to go back in history.

force.description: If the page shows a "Leave site?" dialog because of unsaved changes, discard those changes and navigate anyway. Defaults to false.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__preview_list
tools.description: List servers started with preview_start. Returns serverIds for use with other preview_* tools.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__preview_logs
tools.description: Get server stdout/stderr output. Use to check for build errors, verify server behavior, or read debug output. Use 'level' to filter to errors only, or 'search' to filter for specific text. Use after preview_start.

level.description: Filter by level: 'all' (default) shows all output, 'error' shows only lines containing error/exception/failed/fatal

search.description: Filter to lines containing this text (e.g., '[DEBUG]', 'POST /api')

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__preview_start

url.description: URL to open in the Browser pane without a dev server (instead of starting one by `name`).

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__preview_stop
tools.description: Stop a server started with preview_start.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__read_console_messages
tools.description: Get console output (log, info, warn, error, debug) from the Browser pane.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

limit.description: Max entries to return (default: 50, max: 200).

# 0001 — Multi-country content strategy (Strapi + Angular)

- **Status:** Proposed
- **Date:** 2026-11-21
- **Related:** US-01, US-02, US-03

## Context and problem

The same application and the same build must sell car insurance in Colombia and Chile. Each country has its own regulations, identity documents, currency, coverages, terms and copy, and the business team (non-technical) must be able to change form fields and plans from Strapi without a deployment.

So we need to decide two things:

1. **Strapi:** how content is differentiated by country.
2. **Angular:** how the app knows which country to render.

## Decision drivers

- Add a new country without touching code or schema.
- Each piece of content (a field, a plan) can be edited and published on its own.
- No country data hardcoded in Angular: currency, format, legal age and terms live in Strapi.
- One build for every country.
- Easy to test per country (e2e).

## Part 1 — Strapi: Country as a collection with relations

### Decision

Let's take a **Country as collection** approach, and **FormField** and **Plan** as collections too, with a many-to-one relation towards Country.

- **Country** saves `code`, `name`, `currency`, `numberLocale` (e.g. `es-CO`), `legalAge` and `termsAndConditions`.
- **FormField** saves `label`, `type`, `required`, `helpText`, `errorMessage`, `order` and `step`/`section`, plus two components:
  - `validations`: `min`, `max`, `pattern`, and `validators` with name.
  - `options`: for selects.
- **Plan** saves `basePrice`, `order`, `recommended`, `active`, and `coverages` and `benefits` as repeatable components. Uses native draft/published.

The query would be:

```
GET /api/plans?filters[country][code][$eq]=CO&filters[active][$eq]=true&sort=order
```

### Why like that?

- **Scalable, supports future countries:** create the Country and its fields and plans, without touching code or schema.
- **Independent publish cycles:** each plan and each field has its own publish cycle.
- **No hardcoded data:** currency, format and terms and conditions have a place in Strapi.

### Consequences and tradeoffs

- **Duplication:** each common field, like email, exists as many times as there are countries. On the other hand, that also gives a clear separation of data per country.
- **No atomic publication:** everything has to be published one by one, not all at once for a country. Mitigation: Strapi's Releases (only on paid subscriptions).
- **Risk of forgetting to assign new fields to their country:** Strapi doesn't force fields or plans to be assigned to a Country. Mitigations:
  - a. filter by country in Angular code;
  - b. validate in Strapi on save, using Document Service middleware.
- **Extra code for validations:** Angular must parse Strapi data into code validations, because Strapi only sends data, and Angular should apply strict, typed validations in code, especially for forms and input values.

## Part 2 — Angular: country from the path prefix

### Decision

How does Angular know which country to render? Let's take the **path prefix** approach for its simplicity, e.g. `/co/quote` and `/cl/quote`. The path must always have the prefix.

### Advantages

- **Scalability:** a resolver or guard checks the code against `GET /api/countries`, not against an enum in code.
- **Separation of domains:** a `CountryContext` with a signal can feed each country separately, loading fields, plans, currency and the unique persistent key per country in `sessionStorage`.
- **Easy e2e per country:** just open each prefix.
- **Close to a production-ready solution:** in production, subdomains could be better and preferable, and they could be implemented without changing the current approach much.

### Tradeoff

- Changing the country in the middle of the wizard restarts it.

## Considered options (not taken)

### i18n in Strapi with a locale per country
- **Good:** built into Strapi, manageable from the admin panel, easy to publish and filter via API by locale.
- **Not taken because:** i18n is not designed for this business case; it is for translating the same content. For example, the Chilean RUT is not a translation of the Colombian cédula.

### Enum field for country
- **Good:** the simplest approach, easy to filter.
- **Not taken because:** it has a big problem for this business case: we can't save unique values per country (currency, locale, legal age, terms), which would force us to hardcode data in Angular. That doesn't make any sense.

### A single document per country
- **Good:** everything in one request (a strength, but also a weakness) and atomic publishing per country.
- **Not taken because:** it brings everything at once even if you only need one field, and it doesn't let editors use the draft/publish pattern per plan, only for the whole country document.

# 0001 — Multi-country content strategy (Strapi + Angular)

- **Status:** Proposed
- **Date:** 2026-11-21
- **Related:** US-01, US-02, US-03

## Context and problem

The same application and the same build must sell car insurance in Colombia and Chile. Each country has its own regulations, identity documents, currency, coverages, terms and copy, and the business team (non-technical) must be able to change form fields and plans from Strapi without a deployment.

So we need to decide two things:

1. **Strapi:** how content is differentiated by country.
2. **Angular:** how the app knows which country to render.

## Decision drivers

- Add a new country without touching code or schema.
- Each piece of content (a field, a plan) can be edited and published on its own.
- No country data hardcoded in Angular: currency, format, legal age and terms live in Strapi.
- One build for every country.
- Easy to test per country (e2e).

## Part 1 — Strapi: Country as a collection with relations

### Decision

Let's take a **Country as collection** approach, and **FormField** and **Plan** as collections too, with a many-to-one relation towards Country.

- **Country** saves `code`, `name`, `currency`, `numberLocale` (e.g. `es-CO`), `legalAge` and `termsAndConditions`.
- **FormField** saves `label`, `type`, `required`, `helpText`, `errorMessage`, `order` and `step`/`section`, plus two components:
  - `validations`: `min`, `max`, `pattern`, and `validators` with name.
  - `options`: for selects.
- **Plan** saves `basePrice`, `order`, `recommended`, `active`, and `coverages` and `benefits` as repeatable components. Uses native draft/published.

The query would be:

```
GET /api/plans?filters[country][code][$eq]=CO&filters[active][$eq]=true&sort=order
```

### Why like that?

- **Scalable, supports future countries:** create the Country and its fields and plans, without touching code or schema.
- **Independent publish cycles:** each plan and each field has its own publish cycle.
- **No hardcoded data:** currency, format and terms and conditions have a place in Strapi.

### Consequences and tradeoffs

- **Duplication:** each common field, like email, exists as many times as there are countries. On the other hand, that also gives a clear separation of data per country.
- **No atomic publication:** everything has to be published one by one, not all at once for a country. Mitigation: Strapi's Releases (only on paid subscriptions).
- **Risk of forgetting to assign new fields to their country:** Strapi doesn't force fields or plans to be assigned to a Country. Mitigations:
  - a. filter by country in Angular code;
  - b. validate in Strapi on save, using Document Service middleware.
- **Extra code for validations:** Angular must parse Strapi data into code validations, because Strapi only sends data, and Angular should apply strict, typed validations in code, especially for forms and input values.

## Part 2 — Angular: country from the path prefix

### Decision

How does Angular know which country to render? Let's take the **path prefix** approach for its simplicity, e.g. `/co/quote` and `/cl/quote`. The path must always have the prefix.

### Advantages

- **Scalability:** a resolver or guard checks the code against `GET /api/countries`, not against an enum in code.
- **Separation of domains:** a `CountryContext` with a signal can feed each country separately, loading fields, plans, currency and the unique persistent key per country in `sessionStorage`.
- **Easy e2e per country:** just open each prefix.
- **Close to a production-ready solution:** in production, subdomains could be better and preferable, and they could be implemented without changing the current approach much.

### Tradeoff

- Changing the country in the middle of the wizard restarts it.

## Considered options (not taken)

### i18n in Strapi with a locale per country
- **Good:** built into Strapi, manageable from the admin panel, easy to publish and filter via API by locale.
- **Not taken because:** i18n is not designed for this business case; it is for translating the same content. For example, the Chilean RUT is not a translation of the Colombian cédula.

### Enum field for country
- **Good:** the simplest approach, easy to filter.
- **Not taken because:** it has a big problem for this business case: we can't save unique values per country (currency, locale, legal age, terms), which would force us to hardcode data in Angular. That doesn't make any sense.

### A single document per country
- **Good:** everything in one request (a strength, but also a weakness) and atomic publishing per country.
- **Not taken because:** it brings everything at once even if you only need one field, and it doesn't let editors use the draft/publish pattern per plan, only for the whole country document.

### Decision

Let's take a **Country as collection** approach, and **FormField** and **Plan** as collections too, with a many-to-one relation towards Country. All three use native draft/published.

- **Country** saves `code`, `name`, `currency`, `numberLocale` (e.g. `es-CO`), `legalAge` and `termsAndConditions`.
- **FormField** saves `key`, `label`, `type`, `required`, `helpText`, `errorMessage`, `order` and `step`/`section`, plus two components:
  - `validations`: `min`, `max`, `pattern`, and `validators` with name and value.
  - `options`: for selects.
  - `key` is the stable technical name of the field (e.g. `documentNumber`, `vehicleYear`, `birthDate`). Angular uses it as the form control name, and the summary (masking) and the price rule use it to find values. Labels can't play this role because the business edits them. Unique per country.
  - `type` is an enumeration: `text`, `number`, `select`, `date`, `checkbox`.
- **Plan** saves `name`, `shortDescription`, `basePrice`, `order`, `recommended`, `active`, and `coverages` and `benefits` as repeatable components.
  - **No `currency` on Plan, on purpose:** the user story lists currency as a plan attribute, but a plan can never be sold in a currency different from its country's. Keeping it only on Country removes a source of inconsistency (a Chilean plan in COP) and one field editors could get wrong. The plan's currency is always `plan.country.currency`.

The queries would be:

```
GET /api/countries?fields[0]=code&fields[1]=name&sort=name:asc

GET /api/form-fields?filters[country][code][$eq]=CO&sort=order:asc
    &populate[validations][populate][validators]=true&populate[options]=true

GET /api/plans?filters[country][code][$eq]=CO&filters[active][$eq]=true&sort=order:asc
    &populate[coverages]=true&populate[benefits]=true
```

Strapi's REST API returns only published documents by default, so "only published" needs no extra filter. Components aren't returned unless populated, so `populate` is explicit (never `populate=*`).

### Public role permissions

The browser only reads, so the Public role gets exactly:

| Content type | Action | Why |
|--------------|--------|-----|
| Country | `find` | Validate the URL prefix, get currency, locale, legal age and terms. |
| FormField | `find` | Build the step 1 form. |
| Plan | `find` | Show the step 2 plans. |

Nothing else: no `findOne` (the filtered list is enough), no `create`/`update`/`delete`, no tokens. Permissions are granted in code at bootstrap, so a fresh database gets the same setup.

- **Scalable, supports future countries:** create the Country and its fields and plans, without touching code or schema.
- **Independent publish cycles:** each plan and each field has its own publish cycle.
- **No hardcoded data:** currency, format and terms and conditions have a place in Strapi.
- **Country on/off switch:** because Country uses draft/publish, unpublishing a country takes it out of `GET /api/countries`, so the app stops serving it. Changes to the terms and conditions also go through draft and publish instead of going live on save.

- **Duplication:** each common field, like email, exists as many times as there are countries. On the other hand, that also gives a clear separation of data per country.
- **No atomic publication:** everything has to be published one by one, not all at once for a country. Mitigation: Strapi's Releases (only on paid subscriptions).
- **Risk of forgetting to assign new fields to their country:** Strapi 5 can't mark a relation as required, so it doesn't force fields or plans to be assigned to a Country. An unassigned field just never shows up anywhere, silently. Mitigation (recommended): validate in Strapi on save, using Document Service middleware, rejecting a FormField or Plan without a country.
- **Extra code for validations:** Angular must parse Strapi data into code validations, because Strapi only sends data, and Angular should apply strict, typed validations in code, especially for forms and input values.
- **Named validators need code:** rules relative to today (legal age, vehicle year) and algorithms (RUT check digit) can't be expressed with fixed `min`/`max`/`pattern`, so they are named validators with a value, e.g. `{ name: "maxYearsAgo", value: 20 }`. Each name has a function in Angular. See "Validator catalog" below.

### Validator catalog

The business configures fields; developers own the catalog of rules those fields can use.

- `validators.name` is a Strapi **enumeration** with the names Angular implements, so an editor can only pick a rule that exists. A typo or an unknown rule is impossible from the admin panel.
- The catalog is generic and parameterized, so new combinations need no code:

| Name | Value | Example use |
|------|-------|-------------|
| `minAge` | years (defaults to `country.legalAge`) | birth date: policyholder of legal age |
| `maxYearsAgo` | years | vehicle year: not more than 20 years old |
| `maxYearsAhead` | years | vehicle year: not later than next year |
| `rut` | — | Chilean RUT check digit |

  Plus the plain `min`, `max` and `pattern` in `validations`, which cover most document and plate formats (cédula, placa, patente) by regex.
- If Angular receives a validator name it doesn't know (e.g. an older build), it ignores it, logs a warning and keeps the form usable. The required flag and `pattern` still apply.

**What this means for the requirement** ("change the form fields and the offered plans from Strapi without requesting a deployment"): adding, removing, reordering and relabelling fields, changing required flags, messages, options, ranges, patterns, and picking any validator from the catalog are all done from Strapi, no deployment. That is new behavior, not configuration, so it stays within the requirement.

## Part 2 — Angular: country from the path prefix

- **Easy e2e per country:** just open each prefix.

- A mistyped country in the URL silently lands on another country instead of showing an error. Acceptable because every page shows which country is active.

- **Not taken because:** i18n is not designed for this business case; it is for translating the same content. For example, the Chilean RUT is not a translation of the Colombian cédula.

# 0001 — Multi-country content strategy (Strapi + Angular)

- **Status:** Proposed
- **Date:** 2026-11-21
- **Related:** US-01, US-02, US-03

## Context and problem

The same application and the same build must sell car insurance in Colombia and Chile. Each country has its own regulations, identity documents, currency, coverages, terms and copy, and the business team (non-technical) must be able to change form fields and plans from Strapi without a deployment.

So we need to decide two things:

1. **Strapi:** how content is differentiated by country.
2. **Angular:** how the app knows which country to render.

## Decision drivers

- Add a new country without touching code or schema.
- Each piece of content (a field, a plan) can be edited and published on its own.
- No country data hardcoded in Angular: currency, format, legal age and terms live in Strapi.
- One build for every country.
- Easy to test per country (e2e).

## Part 1 — Strapi: Country as a collection with relations

### Decision

Let's take a **Country as collection** approach, and **FormField** and **Plan** as collections too, with a many-to-one relation towards Country. All three use native draft/published.

- **Country** saves `code`, `name`, `currency`, `numberLocale` (e.g. `es-CO`), `legalAge` and `termsAndConditions`.
- **FormField** saves `key`, `label`, `type`, `required`, `helpText`, `errorMessage`, `order` and `step`/`section`, plus two components:
  - `validations`: `min`, `max`, `pattern`, and `validators` with name and value.
  - `options`: for selects.
  - `key` is the stable technical name of the field (e.g. `documentNumber`, `vehicleYear`, `birthDate`). Angular uses it as the form control name, and the summary (masking) and the price rule use it to find values. Labels can't play this role because the business edits them. Unique per country.
  - `type` is an enumeration: `text`, `number`, `select`, `date`, `checkbox`.
- **Plan** saves `name`, `shortDescription`, `basePrice`, `order`, `recommended`, `active`, and `coverages` and `benefits` as repeatable components.
  - **No `currency` on Plan, on purpose:** the user story lists currency as a plan attribute, but a plan can never be sold in a currency different from its country's. Keeping it only on Country removes a source of inconsistency (a Chilean plan in COP) and one field editors could get wrong. The plan's currency is always `plan.country.currency`.

The queries would be:

```
GET /api/countries?fields[0]=code&fields[1]=name&sort=name:asc

GET /api/form-fields?filters[country][code][$eq]=CO&sort=order:asc
    &populate[validations][populate][validators]=true&populate[options]=true

GET /api/plans?filters[country][code][$eq]=CO&filters[active][$eq]=true&sort=order:asc
    &populate[coverages]=true&populate[benefits]=true
```

Strapi's REST API returns only published documents by default, so "only published" needs no extra filter. Components aren't returned unless populated, so `populate` is explicit (never `populate=*`).

### Public role permissions

The browser only reads, so the Public role gets exactly:

| Content type | Action | Why |
|--------------|--------|-----|
| Country | `find` | Validate the URL prefix, get currency, locale, legal age and terms. |
| FormField | `find` | Build the step 1 form. |
| Plan | `find` | Show the step 2 plans. |

Nothing else: no `findOne` (the filtered list is enough), no `create`/`update`/`delete`, no tokens. Permissions are granted in code at bootstrap, so a fresh database gets the same setup.

### Why like that?

- **Scalable, supports future countries:** create the Country and its fields and plans, without touching code or schema.
- **Independent publish cycles:** each plan and each field has its own publish cycle.
- **No hardcoded data:** currency, format and terms and conditions have a place in Strapi.
- **Country on/off switch:** because Country uses draft/publish, unpublishing a country takes it out of `GET /api/countries`, so the app stops serving it. Changes to the terms and conditions also go through draft and publish instead of going live on save.

### Consequences and tradeoffs

- **Duplication:** each common field, like email, exists as many times as there are countries. On the other hand, that also gives a clear separation of data per country.
- **No atomic publication:** everything has to be published one by one, not all at once for a country. Mitigation: Strapi's Releases (only on paid subscriptions).
- **Risk of forgetting to assign new fields to their country:** Strapi 5 can't mark a relation as required, so it doesn't force fields or plans to be assigned to a Country. An unassigned field just never shows up anywhere, silently. Mitigation (recommended): validate in Strapi on save, using Document Service middleware, rejecting a FormField or Plan without a country.
- **Extra code for validations:** Angular must parse Strapi data into code validations, because Strapi only sends data, and Angular should apply strict, typed validations in code, especially for forms and input values.
- **Named validators need code:** rules relative to today (legal age, vehicle year) and algorithms (RUT check digit) can't be expressed with fixed `min`/`max`/`pattern`, so they are named validators with a value, e.g. `{ name: "maxYearsAgo", value: 20 }`. Each name has a function in Angular. See "Validator catalog" below.

### Validator catalog

The business configures fields; developers own the catalog of rules those fields can use.

- `validators.name` is a Strapi **enumeration** with the names Angular implements, so an editor can only pick a rule that exists. A typo or an unknown rule is impossible from the admin panel.
- The catalog is generic and parameterized, so new combinations need no code:

| Name | Value | Example use |
|------|-------|-------------|
| `minAge` | years (defaults to `country.legalAge`) | birth date: policyholder of legal age |
| `maxYearsAgo` | years | vehicle year: not more than 20 years old |
| `maxYearsAhead` | years | vehicle year: not later than next year |
| `rut` | — | Chilean RUT check digit |

  Plus the plain `min`, `max` and `pattern` in `validations`, which cover most document and plate formats (cédula, placa, patente) by regex.
- If Angular receives a validator name it doesn't know (e.g. an older build), it ignores it, logs a warning and keeps the form usable. The required flag and `pattern` still apply.

How does Angular know which country to render? Let's take the **path prefix** approach for its simplicity, e.g. `/co/quote` and `/cl/quote`. The path must always have the prefix.

- The prefix is the country `code` in lower case (`/co` ↔ `CO`).
- `/` and any unknown or unpublished prefix (e.g. `/pe/quote`) **redirect** to the first country returned by `GET /api/countries` (sorted by name), so no country code is hardcoded.

### Advantages

- **Scalability:** a resolver or guard checks the code against `GET /api/countries`, not against an enum in code.
- **Separation of domains:** a `CountryContext` with a signal can feed each country separately, loading fields, plans, currency and the unique persistent key per country in `sessionStorage`.
- **Easy e2e per country:** just open each prefix.
- **Close to a production-ready solution:** in production, subdomains could be better and preferable, and they could be implemented without changing the current approach much.

### Tradeoff

- Changing the country in the middle of the wizard restarts it.
- A mistyped country in the URL silently lands on another country instead of showing an error. Acceptable because every page shows which country is active.

## Considered options (not taken)

### i18n in Strapi with a locale per country
- **Good:** built into Strapi, manageable from the admin panel, easy to publish and filter via API by locale.
- **Not taken because:** i18n is not designed for this business case; it is for translating the same content. For example, the Chilean RUT is not a translation of the Colombian cédula.

### Enum field for country
- **Good:** the simplest approach, easy to filter.
- **Not taken because:** it has a big problem for this business case: we can't save unique values per country (currency, locale, legal age, terms), which would force us to hardcode data in Angular. That doesn't make any sense.

### A single document per country
- **Good:** everything in one request (a strength, but also a weakness) and atomic publishing per country.
- **Not taken because:** it brings everything at once even if you only need one field, and it doesn't let editors use the draft/publish pattern per plan, only for the whole country document.

# 0001 — Multi-country content strategy (Strapi + Angular)

- **Status:** Proposed
- **Date:** 2026-11-21
- **Related:** US-01, US-02, US-03

## Context and problem

The same application and the same build must sell car insurance in Colombia and Chile. Each country has its own regulations, identity documents, currency, coverages, terms and copy, and the business team (non-technical) must be able to change form fields and plans from Strapi without a deployment.

So we need to decide two things:

1. **Strapi:** how content is differentiated by country.
2. **Angular:** how the app knows which country to render.

## Decision drivers

- Add a new country without touching code or schema.
- Each piece of content (a field, a plan) can be edited and published on its own.
- No country data hardcoded in Angular: currency, format, legal age and terms live in Strapi.
- One build for every country.
- Easy to test per country (e2e).

## Part 1 — Strapi: Country as a collection with relations

### Decision

Let's take a **Country as collection** approach, and **FormField** and **Plan** as collections too, with a many-to-one relation towards Country. All three use native draft/published.

- **Country** saves `code`, `name`, `currency`, `numberLocale` (e.g. `es-CO`), `legalAge` and `termsAndConditions`.
- **FormField** saves `key`, `label`, `type`, `required`, `helpText`, `errorMessage`, `order` and `step`/`section`, plus two components:
  - `validations`: `min`, `max`, `pattern`, and `validators` with name and value.
  - `options`: for selects.
  - `key` is the stable technical name of the field (e.g. `documentNumber`, `vehicleYear`, `birthDate`). Angular uses it as the form control name, and the summary (masking) and the price rule use it to find values. Labels can't play this role because the business edits them. Unique per country.
  - `type` is an enumeration: `text`, `number`, `select`, `date`, `checkbox`.
- **Plan** saves `name`, `shortDescription`, `basePrice`, `order`, `recommended`, `active`, and `coverages` and `benefits` as repeatable components.
  - **No `currency` on Plan, on purpose:** the user story lists currency as a plan attribute, but a plan can never be sold in a currency different from its country's. Keeping it only on Country removes a source of inconsistency (a Chilean plan in COP) and one field editors could get wrong. The plan's currency is always `plan.country.currency`.

The queries would be:

```
GET /api/countries?fields[0]=code&fields[1]=name&sort=name:asc

GET /api/form-fields?filters[country][code][$eq]=CO&sort=order:asc
    &populate[validations][populate][validators]=true&populate[options]=true

GET /api/plans?filters[country][code][$eq]=CO&filters[active][$eq]=true&sort=order:asc
    &populate[coverages]=true&populate[benefits]=true
```

Strapi's REST API returns only published documents by default, so "only published" needs no extra filter. Components aren't returned unless populated, so `populate` is explicit (never `populate=*`).

### Public role permissions

The browser only reads, so the Public role gets exactly:

| Content type | Action | Why |
|--------------|--------|-----|
| Country | `find` | Validate the URL prefix, get currency, locale, legal age and terms. |
| FormField | `find` | Build the step 1 form. |
| Plan | `find` | Show the step 2 plans. |

Nothing else: no `findOne` (the filtered list is enough), no `create`/`update`/`delete`, no tokens. Permissions are granted in code at bootstrap, so a fresh database gets the same setup.

### Why like that?

- **Scalable, supports future countries:** create the Country and its fields and plans, without touching code or schema.
- **Independent publish cycles:** each plan and each field has its own publish cycle.
- **No hardcoded data:** currency, format and terms and conditions have a place in Strapi.
- **Country on/off switch:** because Country uses draft/publish, unpublishing a country takes it out of `GET /api/countries`, so the app stops serving it. Changes to the terms and conditions also go through draft and publish instead of going live on save.

### Consequences and tradeoffs

- **Duplication:** each common field, like email, exists as many times as there are countries. On the other hand, that also gives a clear separation of data per country.
- **No atomic publication:** everything has to be published one by one, not all at once for a country. Mitigation: Strapi's Releases (only on paid subscriptions).
- **Risk of forgetting to assign new fields to their country:** Strapi 5 can't mark a relation as required, so it doesn't force fields or plans to be assigned to a Country. An unassigned field just never shows up anywhere, silently. Mitigation (recommended): validate in Strapi on save, using Document Service middleware, rejecting a FormField or Plan without a country.
- **Extra code for validations:** Angular must parse Strapi data into code validations, because Strapi only sends data, and Angular should apply strict, typed validations in code, especially for forms and input values.
- **Named validators need code:** rules relative to today (legal age, vehicle year) and algorithms (RUT check digit) can't be expressed with fixed `min`/`max`/`pattern`, so they are named validators with a value, e.g. `{ name: "maxYearsAgo", value: 20 }`. Each name has a function in Angular. See "Validator catalog" below.

### Validator catalog

The business configures fields; developers own the catalog of rules those fields can use.

- `validators.name` is a Strapi **enumeration** with the names Angular implements, so an editor can only pick a rule that exists. A typo or an unknown rule is impossible from the admin panel.
- The catalog is generic and parameterized, so new combinations need no code:

| Name | Value | Example use |
|------|-------|-------------|
| `minAge` | years (defaults to `country.legalAge`) | birth date: policyholder of legal age |
| `maxYearsAgo` | years | vehicle year: not more than 20 years old |
| `maxYearsAhead` | years | vehicle year: not later than next year |
| `rut` | — | Chilean RUT check digit |

  Plus the plain `min`, `max` and `pattern` in `validations`, which cover most document and plate formats (cédula, placa, patente) by regex.
- If Angular receives a validator name it doesn't know (e.g. an older build), it ignores it, logs a warning and keeps the form usable. The required flag and `pattern` still apply.

**What this means for the requirement** ("change the form fields and the offered plans from Strapi without requesting a deployment"): adding, removing, reordering and relabelling fields, changing required flags, messages, options, ranges, patterns, and picking any validator from the catalog are all done from Strapi, no deployment. Only a **new kind of rule** (a new algorithm, e.g. another country's document check digit) needs a developer, a schema enum value and a deployment. That is new behavior, not configuration, so it stays within the requirement.

## Part 2 — Angular: country from the path prefix

### Decision

How does Angular know which country to render? Let's take the **path prefix** approach for its simplicity, e.g. `/co/quote` and `/cl/quote`. The path must always have the prefix.

- The prefix is the country `code` in lower case (`/co` ↔ `CO`).
- `/` and any unknown or unpublished prefix (e.g. `/pe/quote`) **redirect** to the first country returned by `GET /api/countries` (sorted by name), so no country code is hardcoded.

### Advantages

- **Scalability:** a resolver or guard checks the code against `GET /api/countries`, not against an enum in code.
- **Separation of domains:** a `CountryContext` with a signal can feed each country separately, loading fields, plans, currency and the unique persistent key per country in `sessionStorage`.
- **Easy e2e per country:** just open each prefix.
- **Close to a production-ready solution:** in production, subdomains could be better and preferable, and they could be implemented without changing the current approach much.

### Tradeoff

- Changing the country in the middle of the wizard restarts it.
- A mistyped country in the URL silently lands on another country instead of showing an error. Acceptable because every page shows which country is active.

### i18n in Strapi with a locale per country
- **Good:** built into Strapi, manageable from the admin panel, easy to publish and filter via API by locale.
- **Not taken because:** i18n is not designed for this business case; it is for translating the same content. For example, the Chilean RUT is not a translation of the Colombian cédula.

### Enum field for country
- **Good:** the simplest approach, easy to filter.
- **Not taken because:** it has a big problem for this business case: we can't save unique values per country (currency, locale, legal age, terms), which would force us to hardcode data in Angular. That doesn't make any sense.

### A single document per country

- **Not taken because:** it brings everything at once even if you only need one field, and it doesn't let editors use the draft/publish pattern per plan, only for the whole country document.

# 0001 — Multi-country content strategy (Strapi + Angular)

- **Status:** Proposed
- **Date:** 2026-11-21
- **Related:** US-01, US-02, US-03

## Context and problem

The same application and the same build must sell car insurance in Colombia and Chile. Each country has its own regulations, identity documents, currency, coverages, terms and copy, and the business team (non-technical) must be able to change form fields and plans from Strapi without a deployment.

So we need to decide two things:

1. **Strapi:** how content is differentiated by country.
2. **Angular:** how the app knows which country to render.

## Decision drivers

- Add a new country without touching code or schema.
- Each piece of content (a field, a plan) can be edited and published on its own.
- No country data hardcoded in Angular: currency, format, legal age and terms live in Strapi.
- One build for every country.
- Easy to test per country (e2e).

## Part 1 — Strapi: Country as a collection with relations

### Decision

Let's take a **Country as collection** approach, and **FormField** and **Plan** as collections too, with a many-to-one relation towards Country. All three use native draft/published.

- **Country** saves `code`, `name`, `currency`, `numberLocale` (e.g. `es-CO`), `legalAge` and `termsAndConditions`.
- **FormField** saves `key`, `label`, `type`, `required`, `helpText`, `errorMessage`, `order` and `step`/`section`, plus two components:
  - `validations`: `min`, `max`, `pattern`, and `validators` with name and value.
  - `options`: for selects.
  - `key` is the stable technical name of the field (e.g. `documentNumber`, `vehicleYear`, `birthDate`). Angular uses it as the form control name, and the summary (masking) and the price rule use it to find values. Labels can't play this role because the business edits them. Unique per country.
  - `type` is an enumeration: `text`, `number`, `select`, `date`, `checkbox`.
- **Plan** saves `name`, `shortDescription`, `basePrice`, `order`, `recommended`, `active`, and `coverages` and `benefits` as repeatable components.
  - **No `currency` on Plan, on purpose:** the user story lists currency as a plan attribute, but a plan can never be sold in a currency different from its country's. Keeping it only on Country removes a source of inconsistency (a Chilean plan in COP) and one field editors could get wrong. The plan's currency is always `plan.country.currency`.

The queries would be:

```
GET /api/countries?fields[0]=code&fields[1]=name&sort=name:asc

GET /api/form-fields?filters[country][code][$eq]=CO&sort=order:asc
    &populate[validations][populate][validators]=true&populate[options]=true

GET /api/plans?filters[country][code][$eq]=CO&filters[active][$eq]=true&sort=order:asc
    &populate[coverages]=true&populate[benefits]=true
```

Strapi's REST API returns only published documents by default, so "only published" needs no extra filter. Components aren't returned unless populated, so `populate` is explicit (never `populate=*`).

### Public role permissions

The browser only reads, so the Public role gets exactly:

| Content type | Action | Why |
|--------------|--------|-----|
| Country | `find` | Validate the URL prefix, get currency, locale, legal age and terms. |
| FormField | `find` | Build the step 1 form. |
| Plan | `find` | Show the step 2 plans. |

Nothing else: no `findOne` (the filtered list is enough), no `create`/`update`/`delete`, no tokens. Permissions are granted in code at bootstrap, so a fresh database gets the same setup.

### Why like that?

- **Scalable, supports future countries:** create the Country and its fields and plans, without touching code or schema.
- **Independent publish cycles:** each plan and each field has its own publish cycle.
- **No hardcoded data:** currency, format and terms and conditions have a place in Strapi.
- **Country on/off switch:** because Country uses draft/publish, unpublishing a country takes it out of `GET /api/countries`, so the app stops serving it. Changes to the terms and conditions also go through draft and publish instead of going live on save.

### Consequences and tradeoffs

- **Duplication:** each common field, like email, exists as many times as there are countries. On the other hand, that also gives a clear separation of data per country.
- **No atomic publication:** everything has to be published one by one, not all at once for a country. Mitigation: Strapi's Releases (only on paid subscriptions).
- **Risk of forgetting to assign new fields to their country:** Strapi 5 can't mark a relation as required, so it doesn't force fields or plans to be assigned to a Country. An unassigned field just never shows up anywhere, silently. Mitigation (recommended): validate in Strapi on save, using Document Service middleware, rejecting a FormField or Plan without a country.
- **Extra code for validations:** Angular must parse Strapi data into code validations, because Strapi only sends data, and Angular should apply strict, typed validations in code, especially for forms and input values.
- **Named validators need code:** rules relative to today (legal age, vehicle year) and algorithms (RUT check digit) can't be expressed with fixed `min`/`max`/`pattern`, so they are named validators with a value, e.g. `{ name: "maxYearsAgo", value: 20 }`. Each name has a function in Angular.

### Limits of configurability

What we found: Strapi only sends data, so every validation rule ends up as code in Angular.

- **No deployment needed:** add, remove, reorder or relabel fields; change required flags, help texts, error messages, options, `min`/`max` and `pattern`; use any named validator Angular already implements; add, edit, sort, highlight or deactivate plans.
- **Needs a developer (and a deployment):** a new kind of rule, e.g. another country's document check digit. That is new behavior, not configuration, so it stays within the requirement "change the form fields and the offered plans from Strapi without requesting a deployment".
- **Known risk:** an editor can type a validator name that Angular doesn't implement. Angular ignores it and logs a warning, so the form keeps working, but that rule is not applied.

## Part 2 — Angular: country from the path prefix

### Decision

How does Angular know which country to render? Let's take the **path prefix** approach for its simplicity, e.g. `/co/quote` and `/cl/quote`. The path must always have the prefix.

- The prefix is the country `code` in lower case (`/co` ↔ `CO`).
- `/` and any unknown or unpublished prefix (e.g. `/pe/quote`) **redirect** to the first country returned by `GET /api/countries` (sorted by name), so no country code is hardcoded.

### Advantages

- **Scalability:** a resolver or guard checks the code against `GET /api/countries`, not against an enum in code.
- **Separation of domains:** a `CountryContext` with a signal can feed each country separately, loading fields, plans, currency and the unique persistent key per country in `sessionStorage`.
- **Easy e2e per country:** just open each prefix.
- **Close to a production-ready solution:** in production, subdomains could be better and preferable, and they could be implemented without changing the current approach much.

### Tradeoff

- Changing the country in the middle of the wizard restarts it.
- A mistyped country in the URL silently lands on another country instead of showing an error. Acceptable because every page shows which country is active.

## Considered options (not taken)

### i18n in Strapi with a locale per country
- **Good:** built into Strapi, manageable from the admin panel, easy to publish and filter via API by locale.
- **Not taken because:** i18n is not designed for this business case; it is for translating the same content. For example, the Chilean RUT is not a translation of the Colombian cédula.

### Enum field for country
- **Good:** the simplest approach, easy to filter.
- **Not taken because:** it has a big problem for this business case: we can't save unique values per country (currency, locale, legal age, terms), which would force us to hardcode data in Angular. That doesn't make any sense.

### A single document per country
- **Good:** everything in one request (a strength, but also a weakness) and atomic publishing per country.
- **Not taken because:** it brings everything at once even if you only need one field, and it doesn't let editors use the draft/publish pattern per plan, only for the whole country document.

# 0002 — Agentic workflow: Spec Kit and 3 human gates

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-11-22
- **Related:** `FLOW.md`, `.specify/memory/constitution.md`, `CLAUDE.md`, all user stories

## Context and problem

The increment must go from a functional user story to QA-ready code through a system of AI agents, with people stepping in at points we define. The flow has to be explicit, justified, traceable and repeatable, and it has to stay as frictionless as possible: every human checkpoint costs time, but every missing one risks the agent inventing scope or over-engineering.

So we need to decide:

1. Which framework drives the flow from story to code.
2. Where the human steps in, and how much autonomy the agents get in between.

## Decision drivers

- Traceability from user story to QA.
- A single, approved source of truth that automatic checks can compare against.
- Detect gaps in the user story before building.
- Repeatable: the same flow every time.
- Low friction: as few human stops as possible, placed where they add the most value.

## Decision

**Spec Kit and 3 human gates**, running in Claude Code:

- **Gate 1 — Spec** (after specify + clarify).
- **Gate 2 — Plan** (plan, ADRs, design option, E2E candidates).
- **Gate 3 — Handoff review** (before QA).

Between Gate 2 and Gate 3 the agents run on autopilot (tasks → implementation → verify → conditional E2E → review → commit), bounded by the stop conditions of the constitution.

### Why this one?

- **Traceable:** Spec Kit offers traceability by using git (a branch and a numbered spec folder per feature), which is good to get the whole path from user story to QA.
- **Spec as source:** this gives a valid and approved point of comparison for the different automatic checks within the flow.
- **Gap detection:** the built-in clarify skill detects gaps in the user story, which saves effort before building.
- **Global context:** the constitution serves as global project context, where we set limits and expected behaviors for agents.
- **Repeatable process:** every time we run the flow it is still the same, because of Spec Kit capabilities and default behavior.

### Why this human gate design?

- **Gates live where they contribute the most:** Gate 1 avoids a typical AI error: inventing scope or writing extra criteria. Gate 2 avoids another typical mistake: overdesign or overengineering. An error detected in the spec phase costs minutes, but in the handoff phase it can cost a new wave of implementation.
- **Every gate has its own criteria and a clear rejection path.**
- **Human revisions are logged:** they are saved into the spec's Clarifications.
- **Agent autonomy after approvals.**
- **The reviewer agent uses a different model**, which reduces blind spots.
- **Every agent has its own responsibilities, tools and skills.**
- **Conditional E2E, approved by the human.**

## Considered options

1. **Spec Kit with 3 human gates** (chosen).
2. **Spec Kit as-is, with a human review after every phase** (specify, clarify, plan, tasks, implement): maximum control, but the human stops the flow 5+ times per story. Not taken: too much friction, and reviewing `tasks.md` adds little over reviewing `plan.md`.
3. **Fully autonomous flow, no human gates:** fastest. Not taken: nobody would catch invented scope or over-engineering until QA, which is the most expensive point to find them.

I wrote [ADR 0002](docs/adr/0002-agentic-workflow-spec-kit-and-human-gates.md) with your content in MADR format. It isn't committed yet. Besides grammar fixes like "any story goes ahead" → "no story goes ahead" and "from steps 4 and 9" → "from step 4 to step 9", I added three things.

## What I added

1. **A context section and decision drivers.** MADR expects both, and I took them from the brief and our earlier decisions.
2. **A "Considered options" section, which you didn't write.** The brief scores ADRs on "real alternatives", so an ADR without them loses points. I used the alternatives we actually weighed or that are realistic:
   - Spec Kit as-is, with a review after every phase;
   - a fully autonomous flow with no gates;
   - our own spec-driven development (SDD) variant with no framework;
   - Kiro.

   Each has a one-line reason it wasn't taken. **Please check this section**, since it's my wording.
3. **Status: Accepted.** You authored this decision, so it doesn't need to wait for a Plan gate the way ADR 0001 does.

## Inconsistencies to decide on

- **Two gates or three?** This ADR says 3 gates. FLOW.md says "two human gates", and step 10 is only called "Handoff review", though it already behaves like a gate with approve and reject paths. I'd rename it **Gate 3 — Handoff review** in FLOW.md: the Method paragraph, the diagram, the table row and the no-AI section. The constitution needs no change, because it only defines the stop conditions.
- **"Spec Kit is not suitable for a team" isn't accurate.** Spec Kit's per-feature branches and numbered specs work fine for teams. What's solo-oriented is our adaptation: one orchestrator session, gates approved by one person, and a constitution with one owner. I rewrote it as "this setup was designed for a solo developer…". The difference matters because FLOW.md must answer what we'd change for a team of 5, and blaming the tool would weaken that answer.
- **"Human revisions are logged in Clarifications" only holds for Gate 1.** Gate 2 and Gate 3 rejections currently appear only in the session logs. A short "Revisions" note in `plan.md` would make Gate 2 corrections visible, and the brief scores "evidence that the person corrected the agent". It's a small addition to CLAUDE.md, if you want it.

Between Gate 2 and Gate 3 the agents run on autopilot (tasks → implementation → verify → conditional E2E → review → commit), bounded by the stop conditions of the constitution.

### Why this one?

- **Traceable:** Spec Kit offers traceability by using git (a branch and a numbered spec folder per feature), which is good to get the whole path from user story to QA.
- **Spec as source:** this gives a valid and approved point of comparison for the different automatic checks within the flow.
- **Gap detection:** the built-in clarify skill detects gaps in the user story, which saves effort before building.
- **Global context:** the constitution.md serves as global project context, where we set limits and expected behaviors for agents.
- **Repeatable process:** every time we run the flow it is still the same, because of Spec Kit capabilities and default behavior.

### Why this human gate design?

- **Gates live where they contribute the most:** Gate 1 avoids a typical AI error: inventing scope or writing extra criteria. Gate 2 avoids another typical mistake: overdesign or overengineering. An error detected in the spec phase costs minutes, but in the handoff phase it can cost a new wave of implementation.
- **Every gate has its own criteria and a clear rejection path.**
- **Human revisions are logged:** they are saved into the spec's Clarifications.
- **Agent autonomy after approvals.**
- **The reviewer agent uses a different model**, which reduces blind spots.
- **Every agent has its own responsibilities, tools and skills.**
- **Conditional E2E, approved by the human.**

## Considered options

1. **Spec Kit with 3 human gates** (chosen).
2. **Spec Kit as-is, with a human review after every phase** (specify, clarify, plan, tasks, implement): maximum control, but the human stops the flow 5+ times per story. Not taken: too much friction, and reviewing `tasks.md` adds little over reviewing `plan.md`.
3. **Fully autonomous flow, no human gates:** fastest. Not taken: nobody would catch invented scope or over-engineering until QA, which is the most expensive point to find them.
4. **Our own SDD variant without a framework:** total freedom over templates and steps. Not taken: we would have to build and maintain what Spec Kit already gives (templates, numbered features, clarify), and the result would be less repeatable.
5. **Kiro (spec-driven IDE):** specs built into the tool. Not taken: it ties the flow to one IDE, and its subagents, skills and context file are less portable than Claude Code's versioned Markdown files.

## Consequences

- **Partial independence of the reviewer agent:** it belongs to the same family of models, so some blind spots are shared.
- **Heavy for small stories:** for a small user story the full flow can be heavy and expensive.
- **The human can become the bottleneck:** no story goes ahead without passing Gates 1 and 2.
- **Built for one developer:** this setup was designed for a solo developer working with an agent, not for a team.
- **No human in the loop from step 4 to step 9:** quality there depends on the reviewer agent and the automatic checks.

## Repository Structure
- `cms/`: Headless CMS built with Strapi 5 (TypeScript, SQLite). Content types, APIs, seed, permissions.
- `frontend/`: Angular 22 app (TypeScript, ESLint), Vitest unit tests next to the code, Playwright e2e in `frontend/e2e/`.
- `docs/user-stories/`: Functional user stories pasted verbatim by the human (`US-XX.md`). Never edited by AI.
- `docs/adr/`: Architecture Decision Records (MADR), `NNNN-<slug>.md`.
- `specs/NNN-us-XX-<slug>/`: `spec.md`, `plan.md`, `tasks.md`, `review.md` per user story (Spec Kit).
- `.claude/agents/`: subagent definitions. `.claude/skills/`: skills.
- `ai-logs/`: exported agent sessions. Never edit.

- **Frontend (lint + typecheck + unit tests):** `npm --prefix frontend run verify`
- **Frontend build:** `npm --prefix frontend run build`
- **Frontend e2e (Playwright):** `npm --prefix frontend run e2e`

content.text:
You don't need a Strapi account. We self-host Strapi (Docker or `npm run develop`), so there's no Strapi Cloud signup. What Strapi needs is a **local admin user**, and Strapi asks you to create one on its first run at `http://localhost:1337/admin`.

I checked the repo and found these gaps before we can run US-01.

## Must fix before the first story

1. **Admin user strategy.** One option is to create it by hand on first run. The other is to have the CMS create a dev-only admin from environment variables at bootstrap. The brief wants a single command, `docker compose up`, so evaluators would otherwise hit the signup screen. I'd recommend auto-creating it. The `strapi-conventions` skill already allows that, so the `cms-developer` would build it as part of the first story.
2. **Docker isn't running.** The Docker daemon is off right now, so `docker compose up --build` has never been tested. Start Docker Desktop and I'll check that both images build and the nginx proxy reaches Strapi. Finding a broken Dockerfile now is cheap; finding it in the middle of a story isn't.
3. **Claude Code permissions.** There's no `.claude/settings.json`. That means every `npm --prefix …`, `git commit` or `npx playwright` that a subagent runs will stop and ask you for approval, which breaks the autopilot between Gate 2 and Gate 3. We need a project allowlist for exactly those commands. Pushing and deleting would still ask.
4. **Branch.** We're on `master`, and the default branch is meant to be `main`. Spec Kit creates a feature branch per story from the current branch, so we should rename `master` to `main` before the first story. Otherwise the first feature branch starts from a branch we'll rename afterwards.

## Needed before delivery, not before US-01

5. **A Git remote.** The deliverable is a repository shared with whoever sent you the test, and there's no remote yet. Tell me whether you want GitHub and whether it's public or private, and I'll prepare it. You push.
6. **README.md.** It's a required deliverable, and it should cover:
   - the run instructions;
   - the dev-only admin credentials;
   - the unmet requirements;
   - the note about Google Fonts receiving each visitor's IP address;
   - the `npm audit` warnings in Strapi's dependencies.
7. **E2E environment.** Playwright currently starts only `ng serve`, but the full flow also needs Strapi running with seed data. The plan for the first story that gets an approved E2E candidate will have to handle this.
8. **Session logs.** Export conversations into `ai-logs/`. I'll remind you again at the end.

Items 2 to 4 are setup I can do now. Start Docker Desktop, and confirm that I can add the permission allowlist and rename the branch to `main`.
